speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It provides for the basic terms and working conditions for employees, while meeting employers' needs to stay competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since it was last reviewed in 2012, the profile of our labour force and local employment practices have continued to evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A review is, therefore, timely to ensure that the EA remains relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: My Ministry, together with our tripartite partners the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF), carried out extensive consultations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The result is a set of substantive amendments that meet the interests of both employees and employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members may be aware that the EA was first enacted in 1968 by then-Minister for Foreign Affairs and Labour, Mr S Rajaratnam.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Back then, managers and executives were a very small part of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There was little need to cover them under the EA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It was more than 40 years later that we started covering some managers and executives in 2009.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also enhanced employment protection and benefits over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we introduced childcare leave and enhanced maternity leave in 2004.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2009, we extended the provisions on compensation for work on public holidays and paid sick leave to all employees under the EA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Recently in 2016, we also introduced itemised pay slips and written key employment terms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Each amendment of the EA is a result of careful consideration by the tripartite partners to meet the interests of both employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As we mark the 50th Anniversary of the EA this year, we should acknowledge the tripartite collaboration that has kept our EA relevant and well-calibrated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will mean that other than domestic workers, public officers and seafarers who will continue to be covered by other Acts and regulations due to the nature of their work, all employees will enjoy the protection of the EA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we will extend additional protection under Part IV of the Act to cover more employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, we will enhance our employment dispute resolution framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first set of amendments extends the core provisions under the EA to all employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include the minimum days of annual leave, paid public holiday and sick leave entitlements, as well as other protections, such as timely payment of salary and protection against wrongful dismissal.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, three groups of employees already enjoy core provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, all workmen – these are our manual workers or blue-collar workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, all non-workmen – these are our rank-and-file white-collar workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, managers and executives with basic monthly salaries up to $4,500.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the proportion of Professionals, Managers, Executives and Technicians (PMETs) rising and expected to make up two-thirds of our local workforce by 2030, it is timely to make a more fundamental change to the coverage of the EA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition to the core provisions, the EA provides a set of additional protections in Part IV, such as on hours of work, rest day and overtime pay.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, Part IV covers workmen earning up to $4,500, and non-workmen earning up to $2,500.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are collectively known as Part IV employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, we will align the salary cap of $2,250 for calculating overtime pay with the new salary threshold of $2,600.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Taken together, an additional 100,000 employees will benefit from these enhancements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As we amend the EA to benefit more employees, we have also introduced changes to better meet business requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, currently, when workmen and non-workmen are required to work on public holidays, employers have only two options.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can compensate with an extra day's pay or provide a full-day off-in-lieu.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will introduce a third option for workmen and non-workmen who are not Part IV employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers will be able to grant them time off for the hours worked on a public holiday, rather than a full-day off.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With this change, the options for non-Part IV workmen and non-workmen would be the same as that for managers and executives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With these changes, all employees will continue to be compensated for working on public holidays.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers will be able to grant time off to all non-Part IV employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part IV employees, who have lower bargaining power, will continue to receive either an extra day's pay or a full-day off if they are required to work on a public holiday.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another improvement for businesses has to do with authorised deductions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, the EA limits the type of salary deductions that employers can make, such as absence from work or damaging or losing goods entrusted to the employee.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such controls protect the employee’s interests but can also inconvenience them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, some companies provide voluntary group hospital and surgical insurance for their employees if the employees agree to co-pay the premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The EA currently does not allow such deductions even when the employees agree.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, employees have to separately reimburse the employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This less prescriptive approach would allow employers and employees greater flexibility to arrange for mutually agreed deductions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, employees’ interests continue to be protected.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, deductions still cannot constitute more than 50% of the employee’s total salary for any one salary period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Deductions for amenities and services supplied by the employer will continue to require the Commissioner’s approval.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third set of amendments enhances our employment dispute resolution framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, salary-related disputes are adjudicated by the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT), while wrongful dismissal claims are adjudicated by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, both types of disputes are often related.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In line with this "one-stop service" approach, we will also expand the coverage of the Tripartite Mediation Framework to include wrongful dismissal claims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the years, a considerable body of cases involving wrongful dismissal claims have been accumulated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They put into practice the broad principles used by MOM that also reflect the consensus reached between employers and unions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The type of dismissal cases that MOM hears include not only those when the employee was terminated by the employer, but also cases when the employee resigned involuntarily.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Involuntary resignation can be considered wrongful dismissal if the employee was forced to do so for wrongful reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, an employer may make work conditions unreasonably difficult, to force the employee to resign so as to deprive him of his employment benefits, and to mask the employer's wrongful behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The wrongful dismissal cases heard by MOM have not been published thus far as there was little need to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These Tripartite Guidelines will contain illustrations of what constitutes wrongful dismissal and what does not.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under the Employment Claims Act (ECA), when the ECT adjudicates a case, it must take into account the principles and parameters contained in the Tripartite Guidelines.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In cases where a dismissal is found to be wrongful, the ECT will order compensation or reinstatement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is no change to the scope of remedies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Per the current practice, the ECT will take into account factors beyond just the wages or maternity benefits owed to the employee, in determining the amount of compensation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Following further tripartite discussions, employers have agreed to reduce this qualifying period to six months, on the basis that it would be sufficient for them to assess a manager's or executive's suitability for the job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is in recognition that performance in a manager and executive role is not so immediately clear, compared to workmen or non-workmen, where there is no qualifying period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a win-win approach, as forcing employers to accept an even shorter period would make them more hesitant in offering employment to candidates they are not entirely sure of.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, employers are required under the EA to accord paid sick leave only if the medical certificate (MC) is issued by the Government and company-appointed doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This provision has been in place since the EA was first enacted in 1968.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the Minister back then made clear, there were frequent absences using fictitious MCs; the Government stepped in then to specify which doctors’ MCs would be recognised by law.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, doctors are registered under the Medical Registration Act and are subject to the Singapore Medical Council Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, there is no longer a need to distinguish between MCs issued by different groups of doctors where paid sick leave is concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given this widening in the recognition of MCs, it is timely to also clarify what hospitalisation entails under the EA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The clauses on hospitalisation have been in place since 1968 and the intent has been for hospitalisation leave to cover the period requiring hospital care.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, certain ground practices have deviated from the policy intent over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, some non-hospital doctors may issue MCs for hospitalisation leave for conditions that do not require any hospitalisation, such as sprains.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To clarify the intent, we will specify in the EA that when it comes to hospitalisation leave, employers are required to recognise MCs only if they are issued by hospital doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers who wish to recognise MCs from their own panel-doctors for granting hospitalisation leave are free to continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hospitalisation leave will continue to cover inpatient stays in hospitals and day surgeries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, the post-discharge period of rest or further medical treatment for the condition that the employee was hospitalised for will also be covered.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are also certain circumstances where we will continue to require employers to recognise MCs for purposes of hospitalisation leave.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Occasionally, the hospital doctor assesses that inpatient stay or day surgery is required, but, for some reason, that does not happen.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There may also be other specific circumstances, such as Quarantine Orders as required by law, which would qualify employees for hospitalisation leave.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will provide for these situations in the Act and regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, some employers have, out of convenience, or even with an intention to cover up for late or non-payment of salaries, asked their employees to sign salary vouchers before receiving their salaries, or to sign on blank salary vouchers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin)   Mr Deputy Speaker, the EA is Singapore’s main employment law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It provides for basic employment protections and fair treatment for employees while meeting employers’ needs at the same time, to ensure that our labour market will continue to thrive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The purpose of each amendment is to make sure that the EA remains relevant and forward-thinking.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As always, the amendments today are the result of tripartite consultation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The key areas of review are providing protection for more managers and executives (M&Es), allowing more employees to enjoy additional protections, and strengthening our employment dispute resolution framework.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After discussions with the tripartite partners, we feel that M&Es whose salaries exceed $4,500 should also enjoy the basic protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also increase the salary threshold for non-workmen so that more employees can enjoy more comprehensive legal protection, including when it comes to working hours, overtime pay and rest day entitlement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, in order to ensure that employees and employers can better resolve their employment disputes, we will streamline the employment dispute resolution procedures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the whole, this amendment Bill is proactive and comprehensive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If passed, the EA's coverage will expand to include higher salaried M&Es and provide additional protection for employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, the employers can also enjoy some flexibility in their human resource (HR) management, which is conducive to create a more enlightened workplace.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In English): In conclusion, this Bill will better protect our workers, enhance our dispute resolution framework and provide employers enhanced flexibility.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will bolster our efforts to institute good employment norms and develop progressive workplaces for our people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I declare my interest as a member of the tripartite workgroup which was involved in working out the areas of enhancements to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The EA was first enacted in 1968 to address the urgent need to accelerate economic growth and ensure a steady flow of foreign investments to Singapore in anticipation of labour market disruptions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The EA created more systematic and stable employment conditions to increase labour productivity and business efficiency to achieve these aims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Indeed, the EA is instrumental in ensuring a stable labour market, a major contributing factor of Singapore's economic growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The EA has been revised regularly and it is an embodiment of the delicate balancing of tripartite concerns to maximise labour force participation while ensuring that workers' rights are protected and balanced against employers' need to stay competitive to create good jobs for workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To ensure its relevance, this balancing act also takes into account the changing demographics of our workforce and the disruptive forces impacting work in our economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Since the last amendment of the EA which took effect on 1 April 2014, I made calls in and outside the Parliament to review the EA in light of the changing workforce profile, rising median wages and issues that needed redress.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And I am heartened that the Bill addresses a number of these issues through two broad thrusts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the expansion of coverage of workers under the Bill; and two, enhancements made to better protect workers' welfare.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, PMEs form about 36% of our local workforce and this rises to 56% if we include technicians, PMETs for short.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This figure is growing quickly and PMETs will make up two-thirds of our local workforce by 2030.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As companies push forward with transformation efforts, we must ensure that the EA provides adequate coverage for a changing workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is important as there remain cases where aggrieved PMEs earning more than $4,500 a month did not have recourse under the EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having a salary cap meant that there was a deliberate delineation of workers covered under the EA and those who were not.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some rogue employers tried to game the EA by making use of the salary cap to exclude workers from the EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Others tried to cause confusion by referencing the salary cap to deny PMEs from collective representation by unions, and for unions who tried to extend and to expand the scope of representation to cover PMEs, although this is allowed under the Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is a radical step forward, given that just a decade ago, PMEs were not even covered under the EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the removal of the salary cap, companies should have no excuse to prevent unions from representing and organising PMEs earning more than $4,500 a month.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I call upon all employers to take this opportunity to work with our unions and the Labour Movement to review their employment practices and make concerted efforts to get all their staff, especially PMEs, within their companies to become union members and be part of the tripartite relationship and framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Protection under Part IV of the Act has also been extended to more rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having come across incidents where rogue employers have excluded workers from Part IV protection by giving workers inflated managerial and executive titles and paying them just above the salary cap of $2,500 a month, I strongly urge employers to scrutinise their employment practices to ensure the workers are not unfairly excluded from Part IV protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also appeal to workers to come forward to seek the union's assistance if they are of the view they have been unfairly excluded from the Part IV protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While there is clearly a need to accord stronger protection for a select group of vulnerable workers under Part IV, there is increasing difficulty on the ground to clearly determine if a worker is a workman or a non-workman.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is particularly challenging as many forms of work now involve a mix of both manual and non-manual work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is a need to keep watch on this issue to ensure that Part IV of the Act retains its relevancy in the changing nature of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perhaps, there may come a day when we will do away with this PME, non-PME, PME bargainable dichotomy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, a series of enhancements have been made to enable better protection of workers' welfare.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In view of the rapidly changing needs of the workforce, flexibility has been provided under the Bill for the Manpower Minister to address undesirable employment practices through the making of regulations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will allow the Minister to respond quickly to curb undesirable employment practices and protect the well-being of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Commissioner for Labour's powers have also been strengthened to inquire into retrenchment practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I believe this will further complement the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower which stipulates the norms for retrenchment benefits and fair retrenchment practices as well as a mandatory reporting requirement for retrenchments and assistance provided by the task force responsible for retrenchment and employment facilitation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, when an employee considers that he has been dismissed without just cause or excused by his employer, he may make representations in writing to the Manpower Minister to be reinstated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Such transparency will help to ensure that employees are adequately protected from wrongful dismissal while employers are not saddled by frivolous allegations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While good progress has been made in the Bill under these two broad thrusts, I have a number of concerns to which I opine clarifications or enhancements are needed in the furtherance of the objectives of the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, with increased volatility and streamlining of businesses, I am particularly concerned about the need to provide greater clarity on the ambit of section 18(a) of the Act which allows employers to transfer employees in the transfer of business undertaking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is a need for the formulation of a set of tripartite guidelines as well as FAQs on the scope of application of section 18(a).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge the tripartite partners to work on this urgently, especially since this section now applies to all workers, including PMEs earning more than $4,500.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, I would like to ask the Minister what support has been put in place to facilitate the transfer of jurisdiction of wrongful dismissals to the ECT to ensure their access to justice is not hampered.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: When the jurisdiction of salary claims was transferred from the Labour Court to the ECT, some workers experienced difficulties in filing their claims, as the ECT processes required the submission of more forms and documentation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Support must be provided to ensure workers' access to justice can be done easily and expediently by the ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, now that there is a one-stop service at the ECT for salary-related and wrongful dismissal claims, it is timely to consider having simplified enforcement proceedings of these claims which are under the purview of the ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have come across quite a number of cases where the worker has sought recourse at the ECT and has successfully obtained an order for the employer to pay him his unpaid wages, but the employer fails to pay up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workers who are unfamiliar with the legal system will be surprised or dismayed to find out that they would have to take additional steps and expend more time and cost to enforce the order with no guaranteed outcomes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At this stage, the worker may not have been paid his salary for a few months or may be even out of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some workers may have taken out enforcement proceedings but these efforts are later thwarted in cases when the employer is wound up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some possible interventions that could be explored include (a) the provision of simplified enforcement mechanisms to the ECT which can help to see through employers' satisfaction of orders for which no appeals have been filed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In cases where employers are unable to pay due to financial difficulties, employers will have to submit evidence for their inability to pay and the ECT can assess and determine if this is truly the case; (b) a short-term relief fund targeted at the bottom 20th percentile of the workforce funded by MOM and operated by the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) for workers who have successfully made ECT claims against their companies but failed to recover payment can be expanded to assist more vulnerable worker groups; (c) where the employer has become insolvent, MOM can also advance money to pay part of the worker's unpaid wages and stand in place of the workers as a preferred creditor of the same level of priority the workers would have had for paid or unpaid wages to recover the advance monies upon distribution of the insolvent companies' assets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will reduce the waiting time for workers to be paid and eliminate the hassle and stress of having to take additional administrative steps within the insolvency framework to recover their unpaid wages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, clause 15 of the Bill seeks to define the circumstances in which an employee is eligible for paid hospitalisation leave.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I welcome the amendment to the clause which clarifies that an employee who is certified to be ill enough to require hospitalisation will qualify even if not warded in the hospital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This reflects more accurately the position under section 89(3) as it is currently worded.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this respect, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister on the following points.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (a) Clause 15 states that the certification must be done by a medical practitioner employed by a hospital approved by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I understand that private hospitals may also be approved for this purpose.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are situations where the employees being treated by a doctor in private practice was accredited to the hospital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Could the Minister confirm that the certification by such accredited doctors can be recognised for purposes of granting paid hospitalisation leave?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Could the Minister confirm that the law does not prohibit employers from recognising hospital leave certified by medical practitioners as well?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are, however, some infectious diseases, such as chicken pox and Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD), which are not covered under the Infectious Diseases Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Will the Minister consider allowing employees who come down with such illnesses be granted hospitalisation leave under the Act?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, if an employee is penalised by the employer for withdrawing his/her consent, what recourse can the employee seek from the Ministry and what actions will the Ministry take against an errant employer?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For payments to credit cooperatives, it should still be specifically mentioned in the EA as an authorised deduction.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is the best assurance of regular collections and ensures sustainability of credit cooperatives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Such cooperatives serve an important social purpose to encourage savings and provide affordable loans to working people while they are members.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This helps to steer people away from loansharks and moneylenders in a vicious cycle of permanent indebtedness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To conclude, while we have made good progress in advancing workers' protection under this Bill and the Bill embodies our spirit of tripartism in striking a balance among our tripartite partners' concerns, we must continue to take a proactive approach to ensure that our labour legislation stays current and relevant in a maturing economy and workforce.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until now, our employment law has this anomaly whereby the basic law on employment matters for PMETs earning more than $4,500 are not actually provided for in our statutes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today’s amendments to include the basic employment rights of PMETs in important areas, such as pay, dismissal, leave, sick leave and hospitalisation leave, as well as employment-related claims, is a right step to take.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill proposes to introduce a new definition of the word "dismiss".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have some concerns about the part of the definition beginning from "…and includes the resignation of an employee if the employee can show, on a balance of probabilities, that the employee does not resign voluntarily but was forced to do so because of any conduct or omission, or course of conduct or omissions, engaged in by the employer".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do understand and accept the intention to include the situation where an employee may be forced by circumstances created by an employer to resign.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I still do have a concern over the broad and vague wording of "any conduct or omission" or "course of conduct or omission", which I fear may create ambiguities and uncertainties and may give grounds for abuse by employees who may have left due to bad blood but who might not actually have been so forced to leave by their employers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill also proposes to provide the right for a relevant employee to lodge a claim at the ECT for wrongful dismissal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any interpretation published elsewhere, including MOM guidelines, is not binding in law in a similar way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is clear from this case, and also anecdotally, that companies have tried to exploit the lack of a statutory definition to give inflated titles to fit the category of managers and executives when the reality of the job scope may be otherwise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I note that the Bill is proposing to allow wrongful dismissal claims to be handled by the ECT under the ECA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my speech at the debate during the Second Reading of the Employment Claims Bill in August 2016, I had proposed that “the Government should consider having one Tribunal that can hear all types of labour-related employment disputes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may also take away some cases from the Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can have a Tribunal that hears claims on employment claims, unfair dismissal and discrimination.” In my speech then, I noted that the then Employment Claims Bill only dealt with salary-related claims, not other types of claims or grievances related to work or the workplace.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I said that there was no specific tribunal to address issues of unfair dismissal or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also said that MOM had in previous years acknowledged that there are such cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In January 2013, the then Acting Minister for Manpower, said that from 2007 to 2012, MOM received annually an average of 70 cases from female employees who felt they had been unfairly dismissed, out of which 70% involved pregnant women.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I had said in my speech then that we should not overlook the issues of unfair dismissal or discrimination but that we should look at the examples of other first-world countries like the United Kingdom (UK) which has been having an employment tribunal handling different types of claims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also pointed out that employment claims disputes are often mired in the context of contending allegations of breaches of employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I said the following: "unfair dismissal or discrimination could well be part of the factual matrix in some of these cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the tribunal handle submissions or evidence on such issues?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may well be unfair to parties in such cases for the appointed tribunals to just ignore arguments relating to, for example, unfair dismissal or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is naive to pretend that such scenarios will not happen and it may be an injustice to employees or employers if the tribunal were to disregard such issues or evidence completely." As per my speech during the debate for the Second Reading of the Employment Claims Bill, I think the ECT should also hear claims on discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the debate at the Second Reading of the Employment Claims Bill, I also said that "…we should set a higher minimum monetary limit for cases before the ECT.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A good indication of a minimum limit should be the median annual income so that employers are less likely to be able to delay a hearing before the tribunal, on the calculation that the employee may not have sufficient resources to pursue the case in the civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, the claim limit should be raised beyond $20,000.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let it cover claims involving PMETs, too, and PMETs with higher income." With today’s amendment Bill, the EA will now cover PMETs earning more than $4,500.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also understand that the ECT is already hearing claims from PMETs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it appears that the limits of $20,000 and $30,000 have not been raised yet.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Naive or lesser educated workers who may not know how best to protect themselves with written evidence of any agreement with their employers may be disadvantaged by such a system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, this means that lay people may not be fully equipped to ensure that their rights are protected and appropriate arguments are made in their favour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may arguably not be fair to the employees.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a possible loophole which the Government may wish to look to address.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps, it may be more appropriate to have a non-legally trained person to represent the employer at a tribunal hearing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even with legal provisions which may set the ECT apart from, say, the State Courts in hearing its usual cases in the Magistrates and District Courts, the ECT should always apply the law as faithfully as it can, so that both employers and employees alike will be treated fairly and in accordance with their position under the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, each party’s legal position under the employment contract must also be fully recognised during any mediation process before that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I remember a few years ago, a client of mine received a complaint of wrongful dismissal lodged by an ex-employee with MOM.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The employee had a record of disciplinary issues, which the employer was able to present to MOM.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding the disciplinary case, the employer had properly terminated the employment contract according to the notice provision of her employment contract and the employee was paid according to what she was due to be paid under the contract.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that such a case was, indeed, a one-off and, certainly, I believe that such experiences should not be allowed to happen under the new regime where claims for wrongful dismissal will be heard in the EC, including any mediation process.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Since its enactment in 1968, the EA has been the backbone of workers’ rights as well as a marker of employers’ obligations.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The revisions proposed in the current Bill will extend the protection offered and, at the same time, bring the Act in line with economic changes since its last amendment in 2013.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The first, changes to the Act from the viewpoint of employers and, the second, the role that the tripartite partners play in today's changing employment landscape.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill has been lauded by many employees who see the extension of benefits proffered under the Act now extended beyond any arbitrary salary cap.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these well-known benefits include guaranteed seven days' paid annual leave, 11 paid public holidays, paid sick and hospitalisation leave, as well as the timely payment of salary.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SNEF, of which I am privileged to be one of the Vice Presidents, was deeply involved in the review of the EA.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Spreading over 12 months, SNEF engaged over 3,000 employers and HR practitioners before reaching consensus with our tripartite partners on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to share with this House the main feedback that employers gave during the review, alongside some of my humble observations and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: First, rising costs in today's global business economy, coupled with the uncertainty of trade wars in the world, place our business leaders in a highly stressful environment where thinning profit margins have to be carefully managed against rising costs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, managers and executives will all receive the same protection as rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is happy to note that most employers already provide this minimum coverage of benefits, if not better, for all their employees.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is in the different ways in which companies manage these benefits that operational issues may arise, leading to some employers having to repackage their compensation and benefits for managers and executives.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Such repackaging may take into account their roles and responsibilities, the demands of their jobs and the workplace flexibilities accorded to them.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For example, with globalisation and 24/7 operations, it is common for managers and executives to travel or work during a public holiday and, in essential services, the exigencies of service to work outside office hours.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Such repackaging will inevitably incur actual or opportunity costs for employers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While the sector is transforming to raise productivity, the increase in overtime coverage would have an immediate cost impact.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: What can then be done to assist employers mitigate the effects of these changes?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that providing ample time for employers to adjust would be crucial.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, employers cannot dally and will need to be proactive and start to take steps to manage their manpower better now.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This can be done through job redesign, better manpower planning and scheduling, multi-skilling employees for flexible deployment and other innovative ways.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employees, on their part, should adopt a more open mindset and remove any inertia they may feel about learning new things, and undertake new responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This may include cross-industry training to better their understanding of supply chain processes, and employees must be ready to eradicate any traces of silo-mentality thinking in relation to their job scope.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I hope the Ministry will lend enhanced support to employers to undertake lean and agile manpower planning.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While the Lean Enterprise Development Scheme (LEDS) has moved towards ready-to-go solutions rather than bespoke solutions to benefit more small and medium enterprises (SMEs), many of the SMEs may still not know how and where to start.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: A pre-LEDS assistance scheme to evaluate work processes and job roles will help SMEs develop their own lean manpower plan and understand which technologies could help them in their transformation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) can also take the opportunity to offer their inputs and suggestions to the Ministry and work more closely with their respective members to provide a cogent and relevant framework.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, if greater acknowledgment and incentives can be given to employers who adhere to the EA provisions, I am sure it will prove to be a win-win situation for both the workers and the employers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: If I may humbly suggest, such incentives can come in the form of one-time tax rebates or publicised awards for exemplary employment practices over the course of five years or such time as the Ministry may consider appropriate.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that some will argue that there is a need to incentivise someone for following the law.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the effect of having such a scheme cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Even for the simple act of driving, a clean demerit-free record can result in so much savings for insurance premiums for drivers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, put forward this for the Ministry’s consideration.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Second, in today’s fast-changing business environment, businesses must be lean and nimble to be able to move and adapt quickly or be left behind.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Consequently, they must not be impeded unnecessarily by rigid laws and high compliance and restructuring costs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The nature of their jobs is, however, changing.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Some may need to be redeployed or face the prospect of being retrenched.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Regional roles may mean travelling over weekends or working odd hours.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, companies are meeting the work-life demands of such employees by providing flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, imperative that management flexibility to develop their human capital to their full potential must not be impeded by rigid employment regulations.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employers are concerned with frivolous and vexatious claims by disgruntled employees as it is unproductive and a drain on resources and time.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While there are, indeed, criminal sanctions provided for the giving of false information in the Act, there is little else by way of compensation to employers who are wrongly accused of breaches by unhappy employees.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While criminal sanctions may deter such wrongful accusations, it cannot make up for the anxiety and loss of time which employers who have been dragged through a lengthy investigative process undergo.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It would, therefore, be important for the Ministry’s officers to continue to be cognitive of this and continue to handle each investigation with promptness, efficiency and even-handedness.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, quite apart from criminal sanctions, there is also a need for a framework to operationalise section 14 when it is extended to all employees and shifted to the ECT.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that TADM is working on this and employers will be briefed on this in due course.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While we await the same, businesses will need to step up and put in place a strong HR system with more rigorous performance appraisals and engage the employees regularly in discussions regarding their performance.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This will prevent unreasonable and unfounded claims from arising.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I now move on to my next point – the role of the tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In recent times, many other countries are reforming their labour laws to make their labour markets more flexible and, therefore, more competitive.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Greece and Spain, which had high unemployment rates, undertook labour market reforms to grant employers more flexibility in hiring, firing and determining working hours to create jobs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Even more recently, French President Emmanuel Macron attempted to liberalise France’s rigid labour laws to allow companies to negotiate specific deals on working hours and pay to reduce unemployment.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, our businesses will operate in a more volatile, uncertain and complex environment.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: To borrow the words of the Minister for Manpower Mrs Josephine Teo at the Ministry's workplan seminar in May this year, we will need an agile workforce, agile businesses and an agile Government.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: An agile workforce will enable workers to adapt to company restructuring and transformation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This means workers will have to pick up new skills and take on new jobs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: An agile Government will be responsive to changing economic disruptions and emerging employment demographics and structures.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: But more important, enterprises must develop agility so that they can navigate the challenging seas to sustain and grow their business, create jobs and boost the economy.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: A key strategy for the future of Singapore's commercial viability will be our brand of tripartite partnership.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear that where employers, workers and the Government come together, there are often competing interests among parties, notwithstanding the overarching purpose of advancing Singapore's interests in the world.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The fundamental precept that there must first be a strong and stable country, before a business can prosper and the individual live well is clear.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, this seemingly simple precept hides away the inherent principle that where there are competing interests, sacrifices and compromises have to be made.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): It is, therefore, by no means a simple feat for the tripartite partners overseeing labour relations and employment matters to have kept the peace since 1968 when the first version of the EA was passed, whilst at the same time canvassing the interests of their respective stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In a Motion tabled in this House in 1998, the late Cyrille Tan elucidated the important basis of tripartite partnership in Singapore, and I quote, "The tripartite framework has served us well.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is the basis of our tripartite relations." "Singapore has succeeded so far because the Government, employers and workers have worked together.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Where there is industrial harmony, there is social and economic development; where there is constant strife, it is difficult for businessmen, local or foreign, to make long-term plans.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: A strong tripartite relationship is not just critical in maintaining this industrial harmony.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is also a key competitive advantage to help us become a developed economy early in the 21st century," unquote.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: That these words made more than 20 years ago are still strongly relevant in today’s economic climate is a standing testament to the wisdom of the late Cyrille Tan.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is important, therefore, for these partners to be ever aware of the important roles they play in Singapore's future and so, accordingly, continue to educate their members on the same, zealously safeguarding the values to be imparted to their members and pick wisely those elected to their respective councils.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, I affirm my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, before 2009, managers and executives were not covered under the EA.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This move recognises that all employees should be covered for core provisions, such as the timely payment of salary, annual leave, sick leave, maternity leave and public holidays.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, there are many other welcomed changes to our EA and much of these have been shared by speakers before me, especially by my fellow Labour Member, brother Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: MOM statistics show the median gross monthly income of employed residents, excluding employers' CPF, increased by 32% from $2,500 in 2010 to $3,300 in 2017.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The median gross monthly income in 2010 of $2,500 was the same as the EA amendment in 2012.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Based on these statistics, the new salary threshold at $2,600 seems to be on the low side if the median salary was used to determine the salary threshold.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It seems that the $3,300 would have been the more appropriate salary threshold.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, currently, under the existing EA, employers are required to reimburse only the consultation fees when employees visit Government- or company-approved doctors if the MC obtained results in paid sick leave.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This, unfortunately, results in disparity in the medical coverage between local and foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, employers are responsible for the well-being of foreign workers, which includes being fully liable for their inpatient and outpatient medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I also understand that while it would not be fair for this burden to fall on taxpayers, it creates a disparity as employers are only required to pay consultation fees for local workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I have made several calls in the past to mandate in the EA for employers’ reimbursement to cover medication, either capped at a certain amount or only those obtained from Government polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would benefit many low-wage workers in SMEs and outsourced industries as they usually are accorded only the basic statutory benefits, as compared to other workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nevertheless, I agree with the committee's position that it may result in an unintended consequence of making employers less likely to hire a candidate in poorer health or those with chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, I would like to highlight the calculation of pay for work on a rest day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am glad that there is tripartite consensus that employers should continue to pay a higher overtime rate if they request their employees to work on a rest day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, should the worker be the one requesting to work on his rest day, the worker will only be paid one day's salary.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without a doubt, MOM will act against errant employers if they ask their employees to work on a rest day but paid as if the work was at the request of the employee.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, in our engagement with low-wage workers, many are not aware of the differences in the calculation for pay for work on a rest day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, given their age and lack of skills, these workers may also be reluctant to report their employers for fear of losing their job.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, to protect the vulnerable workers, it should be a single rate of double pay whenever a worker works on a rest day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Logically, no employer will allow workers to work should he not require the manpower to begin with.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If there is any work, then most likely it is at the request of the employer.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The last concern I have is that the EA has not responded to the emergence of the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us have seen workers working for Uber, Grab, Deliveroo, Honest Bee and many others but we may not realise that these workers are not considered as employees of the company.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rather, they are working for the company under contract for service, and not contract of service.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The current ambiguity for workers in the gig economy when it comes to a contract of service versus a contract for service is problematic.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: MOM defines a contract of service as an agreement between an employer and an employee, and the employee will be covered by the EA and Workmen Injury Compensation Act (WICA).

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, under a contract for service, defined as, when an independent contractor, such as a self-employed person or vendor, is engaged for a fee to carry out an assignment or project, he will not be entitled to statutory benefits or be able to make any WICA claims should he be injured during his course of work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I would like to know the reason why the revision to this EA does not take into consideration this emerging category of workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   The key to having an effective EA is to ensure that the needs of the tripartite partners are considered.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The EA, and its revisions thereof, are outcomes of continuous reviews and consultations among the tripartite partners to strike a balance among differing tripartite interests.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, I would like to suggest that workers are given better medical coverage.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The current EA only requires employers to pay for the consultation fees when their workers seek treatment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, they do not qualify for compensation from WICA for accidents or injuries that occur in the course of their duties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, notwithstanding my concerns, I believe that the changes to the EA are timely and I support the additional protection these changes offer to the workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill will improve protections for all employees while balancing business costs and employability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In an employment relationship, the employer often has more bargaining power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is why unions exist – to balance the greater power of the employer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Managers and executives were formerly excluded from the Act because we presumed that power was more equal at that level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That may have been true in the past, when the vast majority of our workers were rank-and-file.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But today, most of our managers and executives are in a similar position to the rank and file.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They cannot afford to use contract law to settle employment disputes, and they do not have the power to bargain over employment contract terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They should be protected by the EA, just as the rank and file already are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A business that cannot afford to grant these basic rights is expecting workers, and society, to pay for their poor business performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, the way that we will resolve employment disputes for managers and executives will, in fact, lower business costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We rely on mediation and, if that fails, the ECT.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: With due respect to some hon Members, lawyers are not involved, and that greatly reduces costs for both sides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: An effective dispute resolution framework will greatly deter errant practices which will avoid disputes in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That said, I wish to outline two emerging labour policy issues that are not completely addressed by this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first is how the self-employed are treated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The self-employed are exempt from the EA because they are not subject to the direction of an employer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have all engaged property agents, private tutors and taxi drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot oversee and direct them in their work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have no obligations to each other as an employer and an employee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But today, many self-employed workers are subject to control by a counterparty who directs their conditions of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Consider the debate during yesterday's sitting on hawkers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hawkers are self-employed, but they can only work if they sign contracts with landlords to rent their stalls.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some self-employed hawkers signed rental terms that directed long minimum operating hours and other conditions of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The hawker can hire someone else to keep their stall open.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But that distinction does not matter to a hawker who cannot afford to hire an assistant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For them, it is like a labour contract.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I was glad to hear that the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources will ensure that these contracts will be revised where necessary to safeguard the interests of hawkers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, technology and new business models have widened the scope of self-employment, while also subjecting the self-employed to greater control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, if you want cleaning services, you can appoint a cleaning company or you can use a platform which offers self-employed cleaners on a task-by-task basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A cleaner who is working for a company still enjoys benefits under the EA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A self-employed cleaner contracted through a platform does not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Technology platforms have made it easier to contract directly with the self-employed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the United States (US), the JP Morgan Chase Institute found that in June 2016, half a percent of all adults sold labour through the online platform economy, up from practically 0% in 2012.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is just an estimate for one month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As of 2016, about 1.5% of all US adults have sold labour through an online platform at least once.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: All of these sell their labour through online platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Since about 10% of the workforce in Singapore are self-employed, we see that possibly at least half a percent or more of our workforce is now selling labour through an online platform in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Technology also subjects the self-employed to greater control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, although private hire and taxi drivers are both self-employed, taxi drivers are not subject to much control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Taxi rental companies do not care what taxi drivers do, as long as the rentals are paid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, private hire drivers are closely monitored by private hire platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some platforms even promise drivers minimum earnings, provided they meet performance standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The self-employed are made to comply with incentives and penalties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is no protection against the use of penalties, unlike the EA, which prescribes allowable payroll deductions and penalties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, I would agree these workers have signed these self-employment contracts willingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the point of the EA is to give statutory rights to the workers because their bargaining power is weak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, there would be too much pressure on workers to willingly sign away their rights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the landmark case of Autoclenz vs Belcher, Lord Clarke of the Supreme Court of the UK wrote, and I quote, "the relative bargaining power of the parties must be taken into account in deciding whether the terms of any written agreement in truth represent what was agreed and the true agreement will often have to be gleaned from all the circumstances of the case, of which the written agreement is only a part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This may be described as a purposive approach to the problem," end quote.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the point is, a contracting party with power may subject a self-employed worker to the direction of an employer, but without giving them employment benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The worker will agree because they have no choice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must have a policy to address this emerging problem of self-employment that also provides for legitimate business needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Fortunately, I believe the Government is acting on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second issue is how unfair employment practices are regulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Workers must be confident that merit is what matters in the labour market, and not their age, race, gender or other personal characteristics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government addresses unfair employment through the Tripartite Alliance for Fair Employment Practices (TAFEP), rather than through the EA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This allows flexibility to recognise the diversity of legitimate business practices in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it may also give some the impression that we have no commitment to eliminating unfair practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I would ask if the Minister can direct that the ECT, in adjudicating cases, can take into account the employer’s past behaviour, including TAFEP cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is so that an employer who has repeatedly violated any of our labour standards would have a higher burden of proof in ECT cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly support the current EA amendment, which will extend protections to all workers while being cost-effective for businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The EA is intended to provide terms of employment, employee entitlement and working conditions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This ensures employee well-being while providing businesses clarity on the terms and conditions they must provide for the people they employ.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendments to the EA seek to provide core provisions to all employees, additional protection for more vulnerable workers, for balancing the requirements for businesses to operate effectively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is, indeed, not an easy balance to achieve.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the structural changes in Singapore's employment landscape and workforce profile, it is crucial that the EA continues to retain its relevancy and responsiveness to changing labour market conditions and trends.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With global and technological disruption impacting all industry sectors, and Singapore's push towards becoming a digital economy, we will see a greater proportion of PMETs in our workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is only right as these are basic working conditions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The statutory clarity on wrongful or unfair dismissal will also help address ambiguity and inconsistent practices and protect employees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Currently, wrongful dismissal claims are heard by MOM.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Expanding the ECT to handle wrongful dismissals claims will provide employees with a "one-stop service" for wrongful dismissal claims and salary-related issues, which tend to go together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Similarly, streamlining dispute resolution services is also good for businesses as having such services will enable employers a platform to clarify their positions in disputes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the disruptions and restructuring that businesses are going through, jobs are impacted and employees will face greater uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would like the Minister to help clarify if the Ministry and the tripartite partners considered how retrenchment benefits are handled to extend protection to workers while managing the cost impact on businesses?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 4 amends section 27 to restate when an employer can make deductions from the salary of the employee.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendment clarifies when written consent is needed and withdrawn.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This amendment, while ensuring protection of employee interest, also provides improvement for businesses in making authorised deductions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the case when the employee’s leave is not approved or possible as a result of work commitment and deadlines imposed by employers, is the employer required to pay the employee the employee’s gross rate of pay for every day of annual leave not taken?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while the proposed changes to the EA are significant, some may argue that more can be done for employee protection.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must be cognisant that, for many businesses, manpower forms a large part of business cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, with the current business climate and companies facing greater uncertainty and feeling the impact of rising cost of doing business, we must ensure that manpower remains affordable and employable for businesses operating in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendments to the EA are trying to achieve a very delicate balance of extending protection and employability while enabling businesses to stay competitive and create jobs for our people.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A final point I would like to make is on the communication of these amendments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From the various appeal cases I have handled at my Meet-the-People sessions on employment disputes, it does seem that employees do not fully understand the terms of the EA and where they can go for assistance on dispute handling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given the significant number of employees that the proposed amendments of the EA will now cover, can the Minister share how these changes will be communicated to both employees and employers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the proposed amendments, the EA offers more relevance, clarity and flexibility for both employees and employers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But to be effective, employees and employers affected by the amendments must understand the changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Notwithstanding my questions, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Only we humans can do intentional or volitional breathing, but we do not do enough of it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened by what might, for now, appear to be a minor but is, to my mind, a significant amendment to section 139 of the EA proposed by clause 22(a) of the Employment (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The existing section 139 provides that the Minister of Manpower may, in addition to the powers expressly conferred by any other provisions of the Act, make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the EA.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear that "well-being" in this case goes beyond physical safety and welfare to include the psychological and social needs of an employee.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This, in my view, marks a momentous shift in policymaking from one that views employees primarily as "resources" to one that truly puts the "human" back in "human resources" by recognising the holistic and complex needs of employees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is, in fact, a policy imperative, given the changing nature of work in an increasingly disruptive and volatile world.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
