text: At this juncture, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to declare my interest as Founder of Hush TeaBar which, aside from Deaf persons, also employs persons with and in recovery from mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I further declare my interest as a founding member of the WorkWell Leaders Workgroup, a private sector-driven effort by business and non-business leaders to champion workplace and employee well-being as a leadership priority.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Please let me share a real-life example of why this policy objective is morally and economically important.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lewis, from the Hush TeaBar team who now lives with depression and mild schizophrenia, could have had a very different life trajectory if he was protected by such a provision many years ago, against an employer early on in his career who verbally abused him repeatedly with every sales call he made in front of her.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: His mental health suffered adversely through this protracted period of abuse which subsequently affected his employability and quality of life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is certainly not an employment outcome we desire for a contributing member of our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are all aware that there are certain drawbacks to the mechanism of civil contraventions, not least of which is the lack of a public record of the nature and severity of a violation, especially so for vulnerable workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Clarification from the Ministry on the reasons behind its choice of prescribing such violations as civil contraventions is welcome.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This means that part of our workforce will have to grapple with mental health conditions while under employment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, studies have shown that an overwhelming 86.5% of those employed do not seek help for their mental health difficulties.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, Sir, I would like to remind the House that when we refer to employees and their well-being in the amendment, we are also including workers who are differently-abled and non-domestic migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Of particular concern to me is the mental well-being of our 1.1 million non-domestic migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another study found over 20% of these workers suffer from non-specific psychological distress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Just two weeks ago, it was reported that injuries at the workplace have increased.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many studies have found links between occupational injury and psychological hazards.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot make light the gravity of these workers’ mental well-being, particularly given the nature of their employment conditions which more often than not include risk of physical injury.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, even as 72% of employers in Singapore consider stress and mental health an issue affecting productivity, only 51% have emotional and psychosocial programmes in place.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: More specifically, I wonder how many employers of non-domestic migrant workers have psychosocial programmes in place.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is clearly a need to persuade and push for employers to have these support structures in place for employee well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is commendable that the Ministry, in proposing clause 22(a), is signalling a change in how we approach workplace well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I cannot help but wonder if Lewis – or any other employee whose psychosocial well-being has been adversely affected by an employer – would be in any practical position to exercise their rights under this provision?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some examples of such legislative efforts to influence employers have been made in countries like Germany, Australia and Japan, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They appear in different forms to fit the workplace and workforce context.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in Germany, risk assessment and implementation of countermeasures are a legal obligation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These obligations state that work should be organised in such a way that prevents a risk to physical and mental health as far as possible.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In Australia, psychological injuries or mental disorders arising from stress in the workplace are compensable and are commonly referred to as work-stress claims.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, public understanding of mental health issues and the public’s attitude towards persons in recovery from mental health conditions play an important role in creating a healthy workplace.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many employers, mostly local and the Civil Service, still demand for declarations early on in the recruitment process on the history of illnesses, including mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They have maintained that declaration of any existing medical condition, including mental illnesses, does not disqualify a candidate from being considered.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This naturally raises the question of the need for and use of such information.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It would seem that such personal information does not, indeed, contribute to the evaluation process of the application in any material form and instead only serves to prejudice the employee adversely because he or she may feel compelled to lie and not declare any such medical history because of the shame and fear of not being selected; and/or live in anxiety of being judged later on by his or her colleagues should they have a relapse, especially if there are no psychosocial support programmes available within the organisation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An informal check with several persons-in-recovery, including Lewis, revealed that most choose not to declare.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would also like to acknowledge that a fine balance, obviously, has to be struck between (a) such a legal prohibition against requiring health declarations and (b) ensuring that our laws do not unduly restrict social and economic conduct.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just because we do not have any natural resources, because even that would be finite.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s biggest asset is our people because the human potential is infinite.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The world changes rapidly, our fundamental needs as humans – not so much.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the basic needs of food, water and shelter, we thrive and flourish when we feel supported in improving our abilities, pursuing our aspirations and living with purpose.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can come back stronger with setbacks if we know we are not alone.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lewis, from the Hush TeaBar team, has, with workplace adjustments, made remarkable strides in his recovery and is now leading a team of Deaf facilitators in operations and finance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Workplace well-being has a direct impact on productivity and innovation and in the quality of life of employees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Every employee is a member of our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, Mr Deputy Speaker, it is clear that a caring, inclusive and resilient Singapore can only come from caring, inclusive and resilient workplaces.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must always remember "human" comes first when we talk about human resources or human capital.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is a great need to change attitudes and perceptions of mental health through education and legislation, from school through work.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Employee well-being must be an intentional outcome of our employment policies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This may be a journey of a thousand miles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments proposed by this Bill signal an exciting single step towards the direction of inclusion and diversity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to more progressive steps ahead, including those I have outlined above.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this change, all PMEs, who form the bulk of the local workforce, will benefit from the EA provisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other amendments, such as making annual leave a core protection provision and enhancing the regulation of dismissals, are also important features of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With progress comes new limits and unaddressed issues become more prominent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the Bill but would like to highlight two sets of issues related to additional protection for more vulnerable workers and wrongful dismissals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first set of issues I would like to highlight concerns Part IV of the EA, which provides additional protection for more vulnerable workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The key provisions in Part IV have to do with rest days, hours of work, overtime pay, retirement benefits and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this amendment Bill, annual leave would be moved out of Part IV and become a core provision of the EA applicable to all workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a good and logical move, but it is less progressive than it seems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Providing for annual leave is already a common practice and an irreversible norm, so the law is only catching up with reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The tweaks being made to the salary caps for non-workmen and for overtime compensation requirements are more important changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Non-workmen refer to white-collar workers who are not PMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At first glance, this struck me as a miniscule enhancement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Upon reflection and research, I still cannot put my head around the significance of a $100 increase in the threshold.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand the Ministry said this increase would result in half of the workforce being covered, but is this an increase from 40% to 50% or from 48% to 50% of the workforce?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is the latter, it does not appear to be a meaningful increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just to illustrate, annual real wage growth in recent years is around 1.9%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that within two to three years, this $100 increase in salary threshold would be rendered irrelevant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My question is why not take the progressive step of removing the distinction between workmen and non-workmen altogether?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand from former Minister for Manpower Mr Lim Swee Say's reply to a Parliamentary Question by Ms Thanaletchmi in May 2016, this distinction is a legacy issue and the Government’s longer-term plan is to remove this distinction, given the changing nature of our workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was a significant increase, and the $100 increase this time round pales in significance, compared to the $500 increase in 2014.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this rate, how would the non-workmen threshold be able to catch up with the $4,500 threshold for workmen so that the distinction may be removed?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand this approach of gradually increasing the threshold is to balance employers' concern with the rise in business costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the $100 increase appears to be quite imbalanced against the favour of white-collar workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the increase should be more substantial to better protect white-collar workers, precisely because this segment of the workforce has become a lot more vulnerable in recent years because of technological disruptions and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Better still, the Government should commit to a timeframe to remove the distinction between workmen and non-workmen altogether so that companies would get the heads-up to adjust their business costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second set of issues I would like to highlight has to do with the enhancements to the regulation of wrongful dismissal claims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry has said that the tripartite partners would be providing further guidance and clarity on what constitutes wrongful dismissal and the factors for determining the compensation amount.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, how would the tripartite guidelines on wrongful dismissal and factors for determining compensation amount, when they are issued, interact with the adjudication work of the ECT?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What would be the legal status of the tripartite guidelines?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Tribunal be obliged to stay within the limits of the tripartite guidelines and, if so, would not this be undermining the purpose of having the Tribunal adjudicate wrongful dismissal claims?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, how should the Tribunal take guidance from the tripartite guidelines?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Tribunal override the tripartite guidelines in specific cases due to peculiar circumstances?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mental health issues are prevalent in advanced economies, such as ours, and are often under-reported and go untreated because of the stigmatisation and lack of understanding of mental health issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same stigmatisation and lack of understanding are the bases of wrongful dismissals of workers with mental health issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another unjust cause or excuse that the tripartite guidelines should cover is related to sexual harassment, as the threat and actuality of dismissal are often used by those in power to sexually exploit their subordinates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also of the view that in such cases where the Tribunal concludes that dismissal was wrongful due to discrimination or sexual harassment, the compensation and reinstatement of the workers are not good enough remedies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such wrongful dismissals are not merely unjust; they are also egregious violations of workers’ rights and social norms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that the Tribunal should be empowered to impose punitive sanctions in terms of fines and jail time for those guilty of these violations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Disguised retrenchment refers to the serving of termination notice to employees due to job redundancy without treating it as retrenchment so that retrenchment benefits do not have to be paid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the employment contract contains retrenchment benefit provisions, then it would be clear that such cases should be heard at the Tribunal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the employment contract does not contain retrenchment benefit provisions, then I would like to ask do workers in such cases have the basis to claim fair retrenchment benefits based on prevailing industry norms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: False retrenchment refers to the retrenchment of workers not due to genuine redundancy but on unjust grounds, such as discrimination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that in such cases, it is clear, too, that claims should be heard by the Tribunal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Highly paid PMEs would likely be seeking claims for back wages and compensation that are much more than $20,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would seem to be unreasonable and unfair to open up this avenue for redress for these PMEs while maintaining the jurisdictional limit for the claims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, what would be the new cap and why?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Progress brings new challenges and highlights old ones that remain in the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second has to do with wrongful dismissals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is good that the ECT will now hear cases of alleged wrongful dismissals, it would be extremely useful if: one, it is clarified how the tripartite guidelines on wrongful dismissal would intersect with Tribunal hearings; two, the tripartite guidelines contain explicit guidance on dismissals linked to discrimination and sexual harassment; three, wrongful dismissals also cover disguised retrenchments and false retrenchments; and four, the jurisdictional limit for claims be raised to make the process more meaningful for high-wage PMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay)   Changing times and the evolving labour market mean that it is prudent to constantly review policies to ensure that our workers can continue to remain competitive as the world continues to change.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The new amendments to the EA will bring about improved protection and welfare for the working population.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The removal of the salary threshold to cover all PMETs under the EA is a good enhancement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud this move as every worker deserves protection regardless of the nature of work and their income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And, certainly, it is great news that the Ministry is proposing to raise the salary threshold on protection of working hours and overtime pay.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there is an increase in the number of Singaporeans who are eligible for protection, I do hope that the Ministry will consider raising the cap for rank and file office workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, I know of residents, mostly young adults – junior executives – fresh out of university, just got a new job, afraid to offend colleagues and superiors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They draw a monthly salary of about $3,000.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their employers or supervisors take advantage of their situation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I cite one particular account of a young research executive who gets paid $3,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She has to do overtime almost every day on weekdays and on weekends, and if she does not go to office, she has to bring the work home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She eventually resigned, and the employer will simply get someone to replace her, and this vicious cycle continues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the other hand, the policy’s fixation with the number of working hours could also complicate matters for companies that practise flexible working hours and allow employees to work remotely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Incidentally, this working style is favoured by the millennials and also gig workers, so we may expect more companies and individuals to be affected by the new policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had the opportunity to speak to several business owners recently at a focus group discussion at the Singapore Malay Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SMCCI).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One co-founder of a software and design company shared that some of his employees choose to work from home, and he is concerned that their movements will have to be documented carefully, which could lead to additional administrative burdens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, if there is no adequate solution in place to scrutinise these employees' working hours, some employees may take advantage of the situation and report longer working hours, so that they can be entitled to overtime pay, and their firms have to pay them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe clearer policies are necessary when we are encouraging more employers to favour flexi-work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another business owner I spoke to hopes for greater flexibility on mandatory leave.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He personally exercises flexibility and fairness and would even allow employees to take more leave than their contract entitles them to when the situation calls for it, and when it is possible to do so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the other hand, he has some employees who do not have to take leave, but he has to ask them to clear their leave regardless, when he could have benefited from the additional productivity, as he is afraid that he will be penalised otherwise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Ministry will consider the concerns of such employers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): As I mentioned earlier, an increase in administrative duties is one problem for companies that offer flexible working hours and remote working.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another employer I spoke to was concerned about the new policy which allows any medical practitioner to certify an employee for sick or hospitalisation leave, rather than the current approach of restricting certification to a practitioner appointed by the employer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He was concerned that other clinics, particularly private clinics, are more liberal with MCs, compared to the polyclinics and Government hospitals, whose MCs are the only certifications his company accepts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For SMEs like his, even a loss of one day’s worth of productivity poses a significant problem.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, his company subsidises employees’ medical fees, so if the employee chooses to see a more expensive private medical practitioner, this also potentially leads to increased costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An increasingly challenging economic landscape already makes it difficult for businesses to stay profitable, especially the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We do not want to create a situation where businesses think it is more worthwhile to employ foreigners who may be satisfied with lower wages, over Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to help them be more productive and profitable, so they do not have to resort to squeezing their employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are many types of grants in place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Questions I have in mind: are businesses coming forward to use them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we take more proactive measures to motivate and help them to do so?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moving on to disputes and dismissals, it is a wise move to designate the ECT as a "one-stop service" for all employment-related disputes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hopefully, this will shorten the amount of time for the aggrieved employee to seek help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Involuntary resignation of an employee should certainly be heard under unfair dismissals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are many undesirable circumstances which lead to involuntary resignations, such as bullying and sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I hope that the Tribunal will be fair and objective to both sides and investigate each case thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Written consent may also be withdrawn, without penalty in some scenarios, by the employee in written notice before the deduction is made.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what about situations whereby the employee has clearly abused the company’s travel policies, for example, to splurge on services for personal enjoyment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Who can they seek redress from as an employer?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With all the increased functions, the Tribunal now plays a pivotal role in ensuring workplace fairness and protecting the rights of employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What efforts will be made to ensure that the Tribunal is staffed with adequate manpower and resources to address all the disputes in a timely manner?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What kind of training will the mediators and investigating officers receive?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another concern I have is the language that is used for the communication.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some complainants, especially those who are older, may find that they are more comfortable explaining their predicament in their mother tongue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps they may not even be literate in English.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that documents submitted to file a claim must be in the English language.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, a certified translation of the document must be provided.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One question I would like to ask the Minister would be: will assistance be available for those who are less proficient in English?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we are on the subject of employee rights, I want to take this opportunity to ask for more to be done against workplace and employment discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no room for discrimination in Singapore and our employment policies must reflect that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, our minority and vulnerable Singaporeans will have to compromise by settling for fewer choices of employers, and this sort of situation can lead to undesirable and even dangerous outcomes in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope there will eventually come a time when we can do away with the listing of TAFEP-accredited companies, as all or most companies would have adopted an inclusive work culture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The general consensus from the ground, I feel, is that employees are generally happy with the proposed changes, but they are concerned about how effective these new measures will be.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Employers on the other hand hope for more flexibility, and there is also confusion regarding the full range of changes in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, although there is an Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, some employers I met are wondering whether the changes would only cover local employees, or if they would be extended to foreign employees holding similar designations and salaries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are worried about how the changes will affect their business costs and productivity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of the business owners did not know about the amendment Bill coming up, and as a large number of them are in the F&B and retail segments, with high labour inputs, they feel that they could be significantly affected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To assure employers and keep them well-informed of the necessary facts, I urge MOM and the Minister to reach out and engage them proactively.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ignorance and lack of resources could give rise to unintentional discrimination and unreasonable employment practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These can fortunately be corrected gradually through education, assistance and mediation by organisations like TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, when employers are deliberately depriving employees and potential employees of their basic rights, it is time to take a more heavy-handed approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the other hand, we also have to be careful not to penalise the good employers who have genuine difficulties in meeting all the requirements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A good work culture is a two-way street after all, and expecting SMEs and micro-SMEs to accommodate a poorly performing employee would take a significant toll on their existing resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, all our local SMEs are important resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to do more to engage them, understand their concerns and help them out, so that they can do well and continue to provide good jobs and a good working environment to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These enhancements are a product of close collaboration among the tripartite partners, with the aim of ensuring reasonable labour standards for our workers while balancing employers' need to stay competitive so that they can continue to create good jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Those of us who are not involved in the lengthy and relentless tripartite discussions may not be fully aware that the EA has evolved and come a long way in a short time.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As our nation's manpower and employment profiles evolve following industry development and changes, it is thus timely to extend core provisions under the EA to PMEs by removing the $4,500 salary cap.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed change recognised that PMEs should be accorded protection for core provisions.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: For far too long, they have been deprived of the Act's coverage and it is, indeed, a welcome move.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These enhancements will further allow the unions to represent PMEs effectively and to increase the scope of coverage even higher.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Today, rank and file workers are better protected than the PMEs, as core provisions are extended to all workmen and non-workmen.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Part IV of the EA, the time-based provisions, are already extended to workmen earning up to $4,500 a month and non-workmen earning up to $2,500 a month.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While the unions welcome the move, we hope the tripartite partners will relook at the threshold for non-workmen to be increased further, as the roles and responsibilities of workers keep changing along with the constant evolving business environment.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While not part of the proposed amendments, an issue of concern was that the tripartite partners deliberated extensively on whether to mandate retrenchment benefits and minimum retrenchment benefits packages.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: After lengthy discussions, it was agreed that retrenchment benefits are better left to negotiations between the employer and the union, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: A flexible approach would be more beneficial to workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We want to avoid instances where a mandated minimum package becomes a norm, even when employers could pay more.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, companies may not be able to afford it if the mandated minimum package is too high, considering the business circumstances they could be facing.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Over-burdening of companies at such times could end up affecting workers even more.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The subject of retrenchment is an emotional one and has financial impact on the workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Workers are worried that such changes might lead to job redundancies.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I am very concerned that there will be employers who jump in without thoughts given to how its employees might be affected.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These are the unenlightened employers who see workers as digits of cost and not as assets.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I urge MOM to work with the tripartite partners to educate employers and management, and urge them to work with the unions from the onset of planned automation, to take care of their workers holistically, and ensure that they would not be affected as long they are able to upgrade their skills to handle new automation processes and necessary technologies.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: At the recent 44th International Transport Workers Federation (ITWF) Congress held in Singapore, the subject of automation and its impact on workers were discussed.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We heard from our foreign counterparts that automation has led to outsourcing of existing jobs, impacted their wages and caused displacement of the workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We, on the other hand, are glad that the tripartite partners here agree on a pro-employability position.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As we all understand and embrace the need to automate and digitalise, we need to ensure that companies engage its employees from the beginning and to find an effective role for them.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want to see jobs going to other countries due to automation as stated by a dockers union at the recent ITWF Congress.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, as businesses transform and move into higher automation and new technologies, there are employers who may conveniently hire foreigners who have "higher skills" and citing that our Singaporean workers do not have these skills.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: But what have these employers done to train our Singaporean workers to take on these jobs?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We should look at incentivising companies that train their workers to attain higher skills and, at the same time, pay closer attention to how we can enhance our Fair Consideration Framework.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: One of the core supporting pillars of Singapore's economy is our strong Tripartism.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The parties involved must have a shared vision of wanting the nation to succeed.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Only then can we all have a share in the success.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Tripartism has contributed to us being ranked the top 10 most competitive economies in the world and ranked No 2 for being a business-friendly environment by the World Bank.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I strongly urge employers to work with the unions.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not take labour relations for granted.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not forget the lessons learned from the volatile industrial climate of the 1950s and 1960s.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: With this, I move in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The EA is the cornerstone of our employment regime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It provides an additional layer of protection for employees beyond contract law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It recognises that there are certain fundamental protections that employees and employers should not be allowed to contract out of.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also recognises that there are underlying power imbalances that may weaken the nature of the consent in an employment relationship.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is thus important to regularly review the EA to ensure that its provisions take into account the reality of the employee-employer relationship.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this in mind, I have a number of clarifications to make on the interpretation and application of the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there is no definition of what constitutes dismissal without just cause or excuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Without a clear definition, the protection against unfair dismissal may be ineffective because instances of unfair dismissals are often not clear cut and can be easily disguised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Civil society groups have documented examples of such stories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In one case, a mother was told to leave when she returned from her maternity leave as the company had carried out a retrenchment exercise while she was away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, she also reported being "nitpicked" and "mentally abused" by her superior while she was pregnant and strongly suspected that the superior took the retrenchment exercise as a chance to "get rid" of her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In another case, a pregnant lady was dismissed shortly after returning from hospitalisation leave for severe morning sickness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While poor work performance was cited for the reason of the dismissal, the company did not seem to have a problem with her work performance prior to her pregnancy, even praising her for being an exemplary role model.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The odd actions of her employers, such as locking her out of her work email account which she could only access using a temporary password and hiring a new person whose job scope and job title were similar to hers, only occurred after she returned from hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The hospitalisation and one incident of lateness to work, which were both caused by her pregnancy, seemed to have escalated into her dismissal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a disability discrimination case, a stroke survivor with mobility issues was dismissed after a colleague had reported witnessing the individual slipping and falling on the way to the toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide examples of unfair dismissals?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister further consider providing clear definitions of what constitute dismissal without just cause or excuse under subsidiary legislation or as guidelines?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can such regulations or guidelines also include specific forms of discrimination on the basis of gender or disability?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would clarify for employees their rights on discriminatory dismissals and assist the ECT in adjudicating unfair dismissal claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, section 27(1) currently specifies a list of permissible deductions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It appears all deductions are permissible with the employee's written consent unless it is specifically prohibited.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the intended effect of section 27(1)(i) is to permit any kind of deduction as long as there is written consent?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, section 27(1)(c) which permits deductions for meals supplied by the employer at the request of the employee will be removed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be permissible for an employer to now deduct the costs of meals with the employee's written consent?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If that is the case, what is the rationale behind removing section 27(1)(c) if such a deduction would still be allowed under section 27(1)(i) as long as the employee's consent is obtained?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is worrying if section 27(1)(i) is intended to be interpreted so broadly that all deductions, unless specifically prohibited, are permitted with the employee's consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I mentioned at the start, our labour laws provide additional protection on top of contractual consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Permitting deductions as long as there is written consent by the employee seems to be a regression in the protection of our labour laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is undisputed that, in reality, many employees can be pressurised or coerced into giving false consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify whether section 27(1)(i) is subject to any other limitations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, under the new section 27(1)(f), an employer can make deductions from an employee's salary to recover any advance or loan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a potential loophole for improper deductions to be made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether employers will have to maintain and produce documentation of such loan or advance to prove the legitimacy of deductions under this section?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also shed some light on how the written consent requirement will be implemented in practice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm that an employee is only required to withdraw consent before a specific deduction transaction is made, in other words, it remains open to an employee to withdraw consent for a certain category of deduction throughout the course of employment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, what are the penalties and consequences for an employer who penalises an employee for withdrawing written consent?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister consider taking this a step further in future reviews of the EA and Employment Claims Act in reversing the burden of proof where the employer is required by statute to retain certain records?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I welcome the amendments to section 89, which recognise employees’ freedom to consult medical doctors or institutions of their choice without prejudicing their entitlement to medical leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be appropriate to harmonise the positions under the EA and WICA by recognising that the injured employee is both entitled to consult and to have their permanent incapacity assessed by a medical practitioner of their choice.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last reviewed in 2012, the amendments to the EA are much needed, given that there are now many more PMEs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the establishment of the ECT, which oversees salary-related disputes and claims, as well as wrongful dismissal, means that there needs to be greater clarity in defining employee benefits and what constitutes wrongful dismissal.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not a small number, and is likely to increase, given that more Singaporeans are taking on PME positions in multinational corporations, small and medium enterprises and even startup companies that are able to pay relatively well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, as more of our young Singaporeans become trained for the industry, their salaries will set to grow and remain competitive.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, being able to provide employment protection for them under the EA is very much welcome and needed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Annual leave is an established industry norm and it is quite disconcerting that, even as of now, there is still a substantial number among us who work without any annual leave provision.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I welcome this annual leave provision, I question the change to provide only the seven to 14 days of annual leave to all employees, and not the one-year carry-forward of unused annual leave to all employees as well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are those among us who work industriously throughout the year when we are still able and healthy, but who may decide to accumulate their annual leave for a much anticipated and much saved-up family holiday or a religious pilgrimage in the following year.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I understand that such changes for employers to provide both annual leave and carry-forward of unused annual leave to the following year can cause a significant impact on employers’ manpower and budget planning, I urge the Ministry to consider extending the one-year carry-forward of unused annual leave to all employees as well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even if this extension cannot be made in this round of amendments to the EA, I urge the Ministry to consider making this change in the near future.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, I strongly support the move to better clarify what constitutes wrongful dismissal that may require dispute resolution.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I do not have the statistics on hand, anecdotally, I have met residents who have lamented about their discontent with and perception of their former employers for having dismissed them because of some form of discrimination, whether perceived or otherwise, because of pregnancy or maternity leave to be taken, disputes arising out of work-related performance bonus or even claims of forced resignation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recall an incident where a resident was aggrieved that her employer managed to persuade her to tender her resignation through veiled threats and manipulation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was only after she tendered her resignation and talked to friends that she realised she was manipulated and forced to resign, when she could have reported the matter to MOM instead.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the establishment of the ECT and this round of amendments to provide greater clarity on wrongful dismissal, aggrieved employees can at least seek redress and an avenue for investigation into their claims of wrongful dismissal.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From what I understand, this provision has not been amended since 1968, and 50 years is too long to have waited to make changes to this provision.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there may have been instances of forged or fictitious MCs, I believe these are few and far between now.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I trust that our medical practitioners have integrity and will issue MCs only where necessary.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This amendment to recognise and accept all MCs will provide greater flexibility for employees who are unwell to see a medical practitioner nearest to their homes for medication and be given medical leave to recover.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, can this provision also include traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) practitioners who are registered with the Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioners Board?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are increasingly more who prefer to get help from TCM practitioners for their ailments, such as frozen shoulder, plantar fasciitis, or lower back pains, which can significantly affect work performance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These ailments may not have immediate cure but, with consistent TCM treatments, much relief can be achieved.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the need to protect employees from unknowingly signing predated salary vouchers, or the need to protect them from being subjected to salary clawbacks from their employers, for instance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I seek the Ministry to clarify if and how salary clawbacks, for example, can be regulated so as to better protect employees.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Interestingly, a Business Insider article dated 28 August this year declared that following employee misconduct or declining profits, salary clawback clauses in employment contracts are "on the rise among Fortune 100 companies, increasing by 79% from 2005 to 2010".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have there been cases or complaints of employment contracts that have included salary clawback clauses?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Out of these, how many have been couched as disincentives for misconduct or poor performance or declining business profits?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many actual cases of salary clawbacks have been reported to the Ministry even though the original employment contracts have not included such clauses?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I refer to the Minister’s written reply to my Parliamentary Question for yesterday's Sitting regarding the over-inflation of salaries compared to the actual payment of salaries.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry will make further amendments to the EA or tighten regulations regarding over-inflation of salaries declared or salary clawbacks, and take stricter actions on employers who take advantage of their employees in this manner, particularly rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this juncture, Mr Deputy Speaker, please allow me to continue in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More often than not, we see cleaners, despatch riders and security officers who do not have proper and appropriate rest areas.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is mainly because they are not on the direct payroll of the organisations, companies or buildings they work in, and even though they work for very long hours at a stretch, they are always on their feet and without rest.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When it is time for them to eat or take a temporary respite, they often have to find some dusty corner of basement carparks or in rubbish collection areas.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These places are hardly ideal or even hygienic for eating and resting.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure we can provide a better environment and surroundings for our cleaners, despatch riders and security officers, even though they are outsourced personnel and not direct hires in that particular company, organisation or building.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The provision of designated rest spaces and areas for our cleaners, despatch riders and security officers does not cost that much.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I am heartened by and supportive of the many significant changes to the EA through this amendment Bill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, I hope the Ministry will seriously consider the few recommendations I have made.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the questions I have posed and the further recommendations made, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I am deeply concerned about the rising healthcare costs in Singapore and the expenditure on elderly healthcare.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These are issues affecting our healthcare system and have been highlighted in the 2018 Singapore Budget.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: With the increasing burden of an ageing population, along with the surge in incidence of chronic diseases and complexity of chronic disease management, we need to focus on a team-based model of care where various healthcare professionals – doctors, pharmacists, nurses, allied health professionals – come together and work in synergy to provide cost-effective care outcomes in line with MOH’s Beyond 2020 master plan.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we need to empower our allied health professionals, nurses and pharmacists to take on greater roles in the area of minor ailments and chronic diseases management to provide value-based care at a sustainable cost and to actively look into ways to eliminate inefficiencies in our healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This framework came into operation on 1 March 2018 and certifies a practitioner under the national collaborative prescribing assessment framework to be able to review and prescribe independently within the scope of their Collaborative Practice Agreement (CPA).

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This certification is done in a setting that requires the issuing of MCs, for example, in ambulatory care clinics.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: All CPPs have to undergo and pass a three-month National Collaborative Prescribing Programme.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In each institution, a privileging and training framework is in place for CPPs to see patients in a clinic.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Practitioners must have at least three years of experience, with at least a year in team-based care before enrolling into the National Collaborative Prescribing Programme.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: CPPs are regularly reviewed by the Credentialing and Service review committee to ensure safety and appropriateness of care.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: They are also required to maintain a competency portfolio for re-credentialing, whenever necessary.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Nurses under the CPP framework are registered Advanced Practice Nurses (APN) who have completed the Master of Nursing Programme accredited by the Singapore Nursing Board (SNB) for APN training or its equivalent and have successfully completed a postgraduate one-year APN Internship programme.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, CPP pharmacists are advanced practice pharmacists or specialist pharmacists registered with the Singapore Pharmacy Council (SPC) who have completed postgraduate training or its equivalent and fulfilled the compulsory continual professional education (CPE) points for maintenance of licensure by SPC.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As Members can see, practitioners under the CPP framework go through rigorous training, are constantly audited to ensure that high standards of care are upheld and are well-equipped with necessary industry certifications.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, these practitioners can only provide excuse chits to patients.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: If patients require MCs, they have to be directed to medical doctors where they have to wait again for the doctors to furnish their MCs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It causes unnecessary delays to patients and can be disruptive to both the CPP and the doctor.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, most employers accept MCs but not excuse chits.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure that everyone who works will have had to obtain an MC when they are unwell at some point in time.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: You might have woken up perhaps with a flu, feeling feverish and decide that you are not able to go to work that day.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, you would first have to get an MC.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: That would mean going to the nearest private clinic or polyclinic, queuing up with other patients and risk spreading infection.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from being unproductive and potentially spreading your contagion, being out and about would exacerbate your illness when you should be getting the much-needed rest at home.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: One may even conveniently ask for unwarranted antibiotics since they are already at the clinic, contributing to global antimicrobial resistance problems.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It will also create better accountability and higher morale amongst staff because the system had shown them that their employers trust them.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the current EA is not prohibiting such a practice and, in fact, some healthcare clusters and Civil Service organisations have already implemented this practice for many years, but there is a need for MOM to mandate it in the Act so that these benefits can be accelerated across the nation, rather than to let nature take its course.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that there is always the perennial concern of employers – how to prevent the abuse of this system by employees who like to "keng"?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In response to that, I would like to propose creating controls, such as audits and provisions for the privilege to be withdrawn for employees who abuse the system, and a surveillance system to be put in place to ensure that we do not miss out on cluster infections.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In any organisation, there will always be a small percentage of employees who will abuse the system.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The benefits of allowing for sick leave without MC will outweigh the small number of abuse cases.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, even with our current situation, it is not difficult to get a day off from work by faking an illness to get an MC.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Should MOM and MOH choose to adopt my two suggestions, the benefits to patients and our healthcare system will be manifold.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It will help organisations save on unnecessary medical claims from employees just to get MCs for simple viral infections or minor ailments.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The right to issue MCs by CPPs also elevates the recognition of the CPPs’ role.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is a necessary amendment to level up the CPP model to be in line with doctors.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: If implemented, necessary steps will be taken to refine the CPP model in line with industry standards to ensure appropriateness of care.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This will lead to improved patient access to healthcare through right siting of patients and lead to healthcare cost containment in the long run.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Doctors in the community can then be freed up to see more complex patients and be subvented appropriately based on the complexity of medical conditions seen as well as clinical indicators met.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This privilege can later be considered for physiotherapists and occupational therapists to empower them as the first triage point under the new rehab model of care.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These are highly trained Allied Health specialists with postgraduate degrees and at least three years of work experience.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Locally, even if early access is available to these patients, they are required to visit the doctor for an MC.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employment laws are important as they provide a legal structure to the workplace, define the responsibilities of both employers and employees, and outline regulations for resolving workplace conflicts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having current and sound employment laws is crucial as good worker protection and fair rights enable businesses to devote their focus on productivity and profitability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I welcome the extended coverage of the Act to include PMEs earning above $4,500 per month.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our workforce composition has been changing steadily over the years and, in time, PMEs will form a significant proportion of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, it is timely that we extend coverage of the Act to protect this group of workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But more can be done to make clearer the definitions of who are considered employees covered under the Act.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, a worker’s coverage under the Act consists of two main criteria: type of employee and income threshold.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Intuitively, the terms "workmen" and "non-workmen" should be all encompassing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a third and separate category just for PMEs is non-intuitive and can be confusing as to who is considered a "PME" and who is considered a "non-workman".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In practice, the distinction by type and income feels arbitrary as all employees face the same vulnerabilities by virtue of being under a company’s employment with unequal bargaining power.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Moving forward, as our workforce composition continues to evolve, MOM and the tripartite partners should consider removing the distinction between workmen, non-workmen and PMEs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that, one day, we can replace these current distinctions between blue-collar workers, white-collar workers and managers, perhaps, with a singular inclusive term, for example, "employees" or simply "workers".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I would like to highlight a potential problem faced on the ground.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the Act, if working on a rest day is requested by the employer, the rate is doubled, compared to if the work is requested by the employee.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have come across cases where employers have asked their employees to sign statements to declare that working on a rest day is self-requested.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry review this two-tier rate and remove the arbitrary distinction of rates based on who requested for the work on a rest day?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is to prevent unscrupulous employers from abusing the system, just to justify paying the lower rate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The decision whether an employee is required to work on a rest day is strictly a business call.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so required by the employer, the employee should be duly compensated at the minimum rates stipulated by law.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, if the distinction between the employer's and employee’s request is to be preserved, then we should narrow the gap between these two rates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the issue of hospitalisation leave under the proposed new section 89(3).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am glad that the Ministry is proposing further changes to the Act to further clarify the confines of hospitalisation and what would constitute hospitalisation leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note, in particular, that the further proposed amendments would mean that an employee who is certified to be ill enough to require hospitalisation leave will qualify even if the employee had not been warded in a hospital.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to highlight two issues for clarification.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A person contracted with such illnesses may not be required to be hospitalised but will require a longer period of stay at home to recover.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, clause 15 appears to cover only those patients who are quarantined by law.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, what about those suffering from mental issues, such as depression?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), nearly 43,000 people sought outpatient treatment at IMH in 2017.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, employees do get issued with hospitalisation leave if they see a psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nonetheless, workers have raised two concerns with me.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One, sick or injured workers not given sufficient medical leave to recover; and two, reimbursement of medical consultation fees being tied to MCs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Granting of medical leave should commensurate with the medical condition of the sick or injured worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But there had been cases where employers collude with doctors to provide minimal medical leave for their sick or injured workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A medically unfit worker would be at a higher risk of accidents at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But often, they do not raise a complaint because they fear repercussions from their employer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is even often more pronounced if the injured worker is a Work Permit worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, urge the Ministry to take harsh actions against such errant employers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the proposed section 89(7)(A), reimbursement of medical consultation fees can only be granted if the doctor issues an MC.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Workers with chronic illnesses, such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol, have raised concerns that they would not be able to get reimbursement of their medical consultation fees as their medical conditions do not require MCs to be issued.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we are aware, there are some unsavoury practices in the industry that should be outlawed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On occasions, I also host our foreign union counterparts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am often asked if Singapore is pro-business or pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My reply often is that it does not have to be “either or”.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When workers are well taken care of and perform well, businesses will flourish.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We expect companies to take good care of all our workers, regardless of collars, regardless of nationalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The review of the EA is crucial as our economy continues to transform and the nature of jobs and employment will continue to change in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed amendments co-designed and co-developed by our tripartite partners are timely to provide better protection and fair rights to our workers amidst these changes taking place rapidly in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is an exemplary example of the tripartism spirit that we have in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, the stipulated minimum terms and conditions of employment applies to all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern stems from the rise of the gig economy, where flexi-time, temporary jobs are increasing exponentially, with more companies hiring freelancers and independent individual contractors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Based on some of the feedback I had received, there are pockets of workers who are not very sure of their employment rights and entitlements in such hiring arrangements.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, they are at risk of exploitative practices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin)   Based on some of the feedback I had received, there are pockets of workers who are not very sure of their employment rights and entitlements in such hiring arrangements.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, they are at risk of exploitative practices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whether it is overtime pay, timely payment of wages, salary deductions, medical leave or dispute resolution, the Ministry must make a concerted effort to reach out to and educate temporary, contract and daily-rated employees about their rights in these areas.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill is an improvement of the current EA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the Bill does not appear to be updated sufficiently to take into consideration the nature of the emerging workforce in the new economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It also does not incorporate any aspiration for a more inclusive workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, I would like to urge MOM to strengthen the safety net for five groups of employees through the EA and also other measures through its partners, such as the union.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Several years ago, Silicon Valley-based information technology (IT) solutions firm, INTUIT, predicted that 40% of the American workforce will be independent workers – freelancers, contractors and temporary employees – by 2020.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The data that is just distributed today by the Ministry also reflect an increasing trend.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the economy of today, work which once meant years of commitment to a single vocation, to a single career path, to a single worksite or even one employer, is undergoing transformation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Depending on the work arrangements and relationship between a service provider and his paymasters, one can be labelled an employee – a permanent, temporary, full-time or part-time employee – or an independent contractor who could be self-employed, freelance and on-call.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The lines between a regular employee and a regular freelancer or independent contractor, and between contracts of service and contracts for service are blurring and overlapping.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Employees with a portfolio of multiple employers and jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: More entrants to the workforce in the gig or on-demand economy are becoming what management guru Charles Handy call the portfolio employees.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are a new-collar employee group who could be in traditional blue or white-collar jobs, working for several employers and engaging in what is known as a portfolio of jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the new-collar employees with multiple employers, serving at alternate different worksites, on or offline, and expected to deliver work based on either time spent, outcomes achieved or a blend of both time and outcomes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They could be, for example, an IT manager who works for several SMEs or an occupational therapist who spreads her workweek across several schools or clinics, or a cleaner who regularly cleans different homes on different workdays.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In instances, for example, of a medical emergency or a fatal accident, would employees with multiple employers be protected and provided for, or would this duty be pushed amongst the different employers?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These portfolio employees, will they be adequately covered or protected?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What about the skills development of this category of staff for whom no single employer may feel responsible to ensure the relevance of their skills?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can these benefit employees with multiple employers and be delivered through, for example, a coordinating agency in Government or can there be other forms of mechanism to ensure that they are protected?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the staff of contractors who won these outsourced functions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have heard of contracts where employment agents require that they compensate the agency in cases of resignation, on top of the notice required for resignation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Who watches over these contracts and who watches over these workers in the lower end of the food chain?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As more and more work is being outsourced, mechanisms need to be devised to coach and monitor the main labour contractors to ensure that they, too, comply with the employment legislation and the rights of their workers are protected.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on the third group, Baby Boomer seniors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In Singapore, we will see a new breed of senior citizens, those we call the "Merdeka Generation" who are unlike the senior citizens of the past.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These Baby Boomer seniors may not retire at the specified age required.
