speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They may not just head for their overseas holidays or karaoke sessions regularly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead of retirement, they are likely to hit what we call "un-retirement" and will want to continue to be actively working either part-time or full-time in their current vocation or, for some, they might want to seek second careers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government ought to review the assumptions governing employees of this new group of senior workers and better tap on this Merdeka workforce who are generally more educated and more skilled than their predecessors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are (a) our low-skilled elderly Singaporeans and (b) the younger and older Singaporeans with mild to severe disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On the elderly, there are many Meet-the-People Session cases that I have been involved with of elderly low-skilled workers who desire to work but they cannot find work and who are not ill or poor enough to qualify for means-testing or receive public welfare.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are seniors who may not be able to grasp the pace of the new economy and whose manual jobs are readily replaced by robots.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If legislation is also a reflection of the values of a society, is there a further space within our employment legislation to ensure that larger employers, including our Government, set aside or create jobs for the vulnerable, such as these elderly and even the disabled?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I understand the role of job creation may not fall within the direct purview of MOM, but I have worked with Minister Josephine Teo for quite a while and I know she cares for the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I urge MOM under her to extend its influence on partners, such as the union and other work agencies, to create a more inclusive workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, on the disabled or persons with special needs or the differently abled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many terms for them, but I will use the term "disabled", not out of disrespect, but because I will be referring to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I think all these are under the watch of Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In education, legislation has already been enacted to make compulsory education for children with special needs a reality come next year.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is now time to start working on legislating that employers bear some responsibility in recruiting and developing staff with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just as the Ministry of Education has enhanced its special education branch and the education of students with special education needs in mainstream schools through organisation structure and funds.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Other agencies, such as MOM and the unions and other related agencies, ought to step up and focus on this segment of the workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There can be novel ways to include the disabled in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To completely leave it to the Ministry of Social and Family Development to coordinate with interested Ministries and private partners for jobs for the disabled, I believe, is not committing enough.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some countries have established quotas with varying success.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Others have laws to protect discrimination of staff who are vulnerable, for those with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But, of course, it has been found that quota schemes, when not properly implemented, can backfire and result in cheating or just lip service in the hiring of the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, when there is a will, there is a way, as some European countries have found.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Novel and reformed quota schemes that, for example, allow a quota to be met, not just by direct hire, but by working and encouraging an employer to contract with, for example, a sheltered workshop of the disabled for supplies or services, have been seen to be successful.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, these are different ways of including or creating a more inclusive workforce or ensuring that quota and more enlightened quota schemes can be implemented in our country.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have served and seen enough in the disability sector to know that just relying on the compassion of employers will not result in the economic integration of disabled workers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I seek MOM's assistance to take a more active role in including legislation and other support measures to sculpt a more inclusive Singapore workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Start by having Government and larger corporations lead by example and, together with other agencies, adopt more aggressive efforts to aggregate jobs that will allow them to enjoy the dignity of work by this special workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I continue to seek MOM and its partners to walk the extra mile to cater to employees in the new gig economy and also to cater to employees who are at risk of being excluded in the Singapore workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the overhaul of our employment legislation has been a long and extensive process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to see it is finally coming to fruition.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The changes will benefit and enhance protection for all employees.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I feel that, as a matter of principle, we should gradually remove all salary caps for overtime.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If companies need to pay equally for each unit of work-time input, regardless of whether work is done within official work hours or during overtime, they would be more motivated to look into productivity upgrading measures to reduce overtime work.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will be in line with our goal of better work-life balance for all employees.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enhanced productivity also means that our workforce and companies would be more competitive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The result will be a win-win situation for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All these developments will boost Singapore’s attractiveness to investors so that quality jobs will continue to be created for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On this note, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has been quite a marathon because I took the stand at about 4.00 pm; so, it was about three hours ago.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Every one of you have raised important issues which I will address.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But in the interest of time and also in support of Ms Anthea Ong's very timely reminder – the importance of mental well-being – I seek Members' kind understanding that I will focus on points relating to today’s amendments and there are about 40 pages of it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The other points, for which I have about 20 pages, are, of course, very important.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I think they can also be addressed on other occasions, or if we have some time later.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As we debate the merits of the proposals, it is useful to remember the wise words of Mr S Rajaratnam when he presented the Employment Bill to Parliament in July 1968.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a very uncanny coincidence, but that was also the month I was born.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He said, "The Employment Bill should, therefore, be seen in the context of the new problems an independent Singapore faces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There must be a climate of industrial peace and stability to attract both local and foreign capital.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is essential to increase the productivity of our workers, the efficiency of entrepreneurs, so that our products can compete in the stiff competitive export markets of the world.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is the intent and purpose behind this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: How far this Bill will succeed in its purpose will depend on both workers and employers placing national interests before sectional interests." Sir, although five decades have since passed, the fundamentals have not changed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, the EA is our main but not the only employment-related legislation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It works in concert with other important pieces of legislation, such as the Workplace Safety and Health Act, the Work Injury Compensation Act, the Retirement and Re-employment Act, the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And all these to advance the interests of our workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, besides laws, our unique brand of tripartism also relies on the Tripartite Guidelines, Standards and Advisories to promote fair and progressive practices, while ensuring good employment outcomes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, in everything we do, the tripartite partners strive to be pro-worker and pro-business.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This has been a cornerstone guiding employment practices in Singapore that has served us well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As we debate EA changes, bear in mind also that the tripartite partners are always in an ongoing conversation about other areas that may see further changes in the coming years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Fifth, the Government also plays its part for local workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the provision of healthcare, for example, employers' major contribution is through the CPF which builds up our MediSave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government’s efforts include the development of public healthcare facilities and schemes like MediShield Life, CareShield Life and Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS), which together, keep healthcare affordable without placing excessive burdens on individuals and employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I hope Members can keep these points in mind as I address the specific concerns.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked for the distinction between workmen, non-workmen and managers and executives to be removed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At workplaces, the lines between workmen, non-workmen and managers and executives are, indeed, blurring.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the EA, the distinction remains largely in Part IV.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Among other things, Part IV regulates working hours, rest days and overtime (OT) payments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Including the more than 700,000 managers and executives whose work is much more varied and tends to be more outcome-based, will make our laws much more rigid and prescriptive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Dennis Tan’s point on defining managers and executives, given that employment practices evolve constantly, the current approach of referring to managers and executives as those “employed in a managerial or executive position” while taking reference from case law works well for the tripartite partners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a High Court ruling earlier this year, it was also made clear that the actual work requirements and individual circumstances matter more than the job title given.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there are already some parameters we work within and they generally work well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Within Part IV, the coverage for workmen and non-workmen has been different since the EA was first enacted in 1968.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Workmen, who are manual workers, generally need more protection where OT is concerned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zainal Sapari, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Arasu Duraisamy and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked if the salary threshold for non-workmen could be higher or even removed completely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That said, in every EA amendment, the tripartite partners consider carefully the impact on both workers and employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When benefits are upped, so, too, are the costs borne by employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, former Nominated Member Assoc Prof Randolph Tan wrote an op-ed expressing some concern about the timing of this round of EA enhancements, whether businesses could absorb the impact in the current economic climate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Douglas Foo also pointed this out in his op-ed published in The Straits Times yesterday and when he spoke earlier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Thankfully, in Singapore, our union leaders recognise the need to consider the package of improvements and not just individual items.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They know it is equally important to give employers time to adjust to changes that come from many directions, not just the EA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The tripartite partners are mindful that changes should not inadvertently affect workers’ employability.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They reached a consensus that these shifts are sufficiently well-calibrated and remain committed to review the thresholds in future amendments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zainal Sapari, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Denise Phua raised concerns about protections for SEPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By their very nature, SEPs do not have the same kind of relationship with their service buyers as that between employees and employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is the main reason we do not attempt to regulate SEPs’ relationship with service providers under the EA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier this year, a tripartite workgroup formed by MOM had put forward a set of recommendations to address SEPs’ common challenges, some of which were outlined in earlier speeches.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And in the earlier circulation of materials, I believe not only a summary of the EA changes were distributed; there was another separate circular that outlined the recommendations of the tripartite workgroup.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At MOM's Committee of Supply (COS) debate in March, I announced the Government’s acceptance of the recommendations and our implementation plan.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am pleased to share that we are making good progress and will update Members at a later date.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Assoc Prof Walter Theseira’s point, we recognise that workers can, indeed, be wrongly classified as SEPs to avoid EA obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Anyone unsure of his employment status should approach MOM so that an appropriate determination can be made.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mischievous employers should take note and realise that they can be prosecuted for non-provision of salaries and benefits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Melvin Yong suggested double pay for work on a rest day, regardless of who requested for it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The double rate discourages employers from asking employees to work excessively.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the other hand, the single rate if workers request to work on rest days, ensures that workers are not inadvertently encouraged to work excessively for the double pay, when actually they should be resting.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zainal Sapari is, of course, concerned that the employees do not always know that they are due to be paid at the double rate if their employers ask them to work on their rest day.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Melvin Yong worries that these workers are forced or deceived into declaring these as self-requested.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM is keen to partner NTUC to strengthen outreach for the WorkRight initiative to educate employers and employees about their responsibilities and rights.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This would also address Ms Joan Pereira's concerns and raise awareness amongst the employees who have not been paid the right amounts to submit a mediation request to TADM.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar asked if the carry-forward specific provision for unused annual leave can be extended to all employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Jessica Tan also asked if an employer is required to pay the employee for unutilised annual leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To clarify, annual leave provisions in section 88A used to be in Part IV and now apply to all employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the employers’ obligation to carry forward unutilised annual leave to the next year remains for Part IV employees only.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The tripartite partners decided against extending the carry-forward provision to all employees which now include higher earning managers and executives – no more limit.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is out of concern for the otherwise drastic impact on business liabilities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members who are familiar with HR practices know that, actually, you have to set aside the liability and factor it as a cost in your books, so there is a real impact.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Annual leave should be planned ahead of time to meet both employee and organisational needs, to avoid situations of unconsumed leave entitlements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the employer is unable to approve leave due to work exigencies and the employee has shown reasonable efforts to adjust his leave plans to suit organisational needs, the employer should allow for leave encashment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is so that the employee can benefit from his statutory leave entitlement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Saktiandi Supaat’s question, there is no need for the employer to force the employee to take leave if an employee does not want to utilise his leave entitlements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we do encourage workers to take their annual leave to rest and recharge from their work to maintain their mental well-being.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A small number of doctors have dual registration under the Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioners Act (TCMPA) and the Medical Registration Act (MRA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the purposes of granting paid sick leave, employers are required to recognise the MCs issued by such practitioners in their capacity as doctors under MRA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Irene Quay asked that we also require employers to recognise the MCs issued by CPPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, as CPPs are not registered under MRA, MOH does not allow them to issue MCs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We understand that MOH will need time to assess the programme as well as other new models of care before deciding whether other healthcare professionals can be certified to issue MCs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOH will, therefore, continue to monitor these developments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Irene Quay also asked that we encourage employers to allow for up to three non-consecutive days of sick leave without MC per year and she gave many good reasons why this would be a more productive approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we recognise the Member's call for this to be mandated, Ms Irene Quay herself also rightly pointed out that employers would need to create controls, surveillance and audit systems to ensure that their employees do not abuse the system.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the EA does not prohibit employers from doing so already, progressive companies are free to go ahead to offer this as part of their talent attraction and retention strategies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to give them flexibility to decide what works best for them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Melvin Yong asked for clarifications regarding hospitalisation leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, employers are not required under the EA to recognise an MC from private doctors, other than their own panel doctors, for purposes of paid sick leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Patrick Tay’s question, employers can recognise MCs for purposes of granting hospitalisation leave from any doctor in the private hospital.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, there is no evidence today that employers have refused to recognise MCs from approved hospitals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We expect that employers will continue to recognise MCs from all approved hospitals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For MCs issued by non-hospital doctors, such as GPs, employers are required by law to recognise the MC for purpose of granting paid sick leave up to 14 days.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Employers are free, of course, to grant additional paid sick leave beyond the annual 14-day entitlement should an employee need it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And we have come across many cases where the employers, out of goodness of their hearts, extend this when the employees do need it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Turning to clarifications on authorised deductions, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Patrick Tay asked about the implementation and safeguards for authorised deductions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As is the case today, employers must provide proper documentation to prove the legitimacy of deductions, if they are for the recovery of any advance and loan.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Patrick Tay's comment on the deduction for payment to a cooperative society, this still remains as an authorised deduction under section 27(1)(j).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the question of whether section 27(1)(i) is limited by prohibited deductions in other statutes, the answer is yes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was Mr Louis Ng's question, I think.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead, the consent must be given specifically for a particular deduction that the employee has agreed to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Written consent given by an employee under duress will not count as valid consent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The employer must also maintain proper records to substantiate the written consent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An employer who penalises an employee for withdrawing consent may also be liable to be prosecuted under the EA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Regulations to protect the well-being of the employee.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar raised the issue of over-inflating salaries declared or clawing back salaries from rank and file workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our law today already allows us to take action against errant employers in this regard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the employer falsely declares the salary of a foreign worker to qualify for a higher work pass, the employer can be prosecuted for false declaration under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act (EMFA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such an employer may also be prosecuted under the EA for non-payment of salary if he pays the local or foreign worker a lower salary than what is declared, for example, in the key employment terms or payslips or in the In-Principle Approval that was given to the employee.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As for “salary claw back” cases being on the rise among Fortune 100 companies, we have not received such complaints from employees, but we will continue to monitor the situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked why violations under the new section 139(2)(aa) are civil contraventions and not offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To clarify, the Minister has the power to provide that violations of regulations are either criminal offences or civil contraventions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Civil contraventions allow us to treat less severe breaches as non-criminal infringements which attract a financial penalty.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Compared to non-payment of salary, which is a criminal offence, requiring an employee to sign on a blank salary voucher is a less severe breach, which should attract correspondingly less severe penalties.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan asked for clarification on what constitutes dismissal without just cause or excuse.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked how the Tripartite Guidelines on Wrongful Dismissal and factors for determining compensation amounts will interact with the adjudication work of the ECT.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dismissal because of poor performance, misconduct and redundancy are not considered wrongful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I mentioned earlier, wrongful dismissal is not a new provision in the EA and there are many cases we can draw reference from.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM will publish a set of Tripartite Guidelines on Wrongful Dismissal which the ECT must take into account.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It would not be possible to define all scenarios of what constitutes wrongful dismissal and what does not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead, a more feasible approach is to use illustrations and set out principles and parameters that the ECT must take into account when adjudicating cases.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An example of what constitutes wrongful dismissal is if an employer dismisses an employee to punish him or her for exercising a right, such as submitting a mediation request to MOM or reporting the company to MOM for an EA offence, even though he or she has performed satisfactorily at work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the case reported by Dr Intan Mokhtar where the employee felt that she had been forced to resign, a claim can still be lodged with TADM.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If unresolved through mediation, the case can be escalated to the ECT and the same applies to persons who believe they had been dismissed due to discrimination.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Dennis Tan also asked if the ECT claim limit would be increased, given that we will be covering highly paid managers and executives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The claim limits are established as such because the ECT is meant to be an expeditious and affordable channel for resolving disputes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Cases involving higher claim amounts are likely to be more complicated and, hence, take more time and workers with claims exceeding these limits can continue to pursue their claims in the higher Courts, where it is probably the more appropriate place to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Several Members asked how the adjudication of wrongful dismissals at the ECT will work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Douglas Foo asked if there are any measures to prevent frivolous claims of wrongful dismissal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Dennis Tan spoke about possible abuse of this recourse by disgruntled employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are reasonable concerns that employers generally have, now that more managers and executives are covered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Employees who feel that they have been wrongfully dismissed may first submit a request to for mediation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: TADM will do its part to prevent frivolous and unmeritorious cases from proceeding.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For cases of contractual termination, where the employer has met all his obligations, TADM will first ensure that there is a case for the employer to answer before contacting the employer to attend mediation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The employee will have to substantiate why he or she thinks that dismissal was wrongful, for example, by citing specific incidents which gave rise to the claim.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For cases like the staff who took advantage of staff travel privileges which Mr Saktiandi Supaat mentioned, if the employer has established such abuse after due inquiry, the employer can dismiss the employee without notice on grounds of misconduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Patrick Tay asked what support has been put in place to facilitate the transfer of the adjudication of wrongful dismissal claims from MOM to ECT.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: ECT and TADM, where compulsory pre-ECT mediation takes place, will be expanding their manpower to meet the new demands.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These mediators and investigation officers involved undergo training programmes that have been designed to equip them with the relevant skills.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked if adverse inferences may be drawn against employers if they fail to produce documents, such as Key Employment Terms and salary slips, and also employer's past behaviour.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to whether we will consider reversing the burden of proof for salary claims, we are mindful that reversing the burden of proof for such cases may result in opportunistic employees filing frivolous claims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we would not do so for now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how the Ministry will be communicating the changes to the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Actually, I think Ms Joan Pereira also mentioned this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM will be publishing an online guidebook shortly, summarising the key amendments to the EA, along with how employers should review their existing HR policies to ensure compliance with the Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are also working with SNEF, NTUC and other industry partners to hold briefings on the EA amendments over the next few months, prior to the implementation on 1 April 2019.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They have asked how the EA will cater to the changing workforce, where employees may be more mobile, and have multiple employers – the portfolio workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As mentioned, we have other tools that complement the EA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member mentioned the need to better protect outsourced workers who, by the way, are still employed by the outsourced service provider which has employer obligations towards the employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides the protection already afforded to them under the EA, the Tripartite Standard on Employment of Term Contract Employees will help bring about better employment conditions for such workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Once again, Sir, I thank Members of the House for their support of this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope that I have addressed questions and suggestions related to today's amendments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The other points remain important and can be addressed at other platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For this amendment, the tripartite discussions started quite early in the tenure of former Manpower Minister Lim Swee Say – and he is seated right there – and was followed through when I took over from him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members can be certain that as soon as we start to implement today's changes, we will again be looking forward as to what more is needed for the future, and whether the person standing here to pass those next sets of amendments will be me or someone else – who can tell?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Building a tripartite consensus on what are the right changes to make, and when to make them, which employee groups to focus on in each amendment, all these deliberations take a great amount of time and effort that is often unseen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I might add that it takes a lot of mutual trust among the tripartite partners, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yet, this is also our greatest strength that has ensured improvements are sustainable, with no drastic U-turns every now and then, which you see in other countries – what one government promises, and then the next government comes and says they are not valid anymore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have not seen that throughout the course of the EA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This strength is also mentioned by many Members of Parliament, notably, Mr Douglas Foo, Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Arasu Duraisamy, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a result, we have helped our businesses to continue providing good jobs and the vast majority of our workers to enjoy good employment outcomes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM is deeply grateful to the many stakeholders in the tripartite partnership that have made possible today's changes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They have worked tirelessly to make this a reality.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you want to clarify something?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Just two points of clarification with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I know it is taking our time but there are two points.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I hope the Ministry and the tripartite partners can look at the enforcement of the ECT judgments so that we have expedient and also speedy resolution and ease of resolution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I spoke about it and I hope the tripartite partners will work together to come up with a set of frequently asked questions and guidelines to give greater clarity before the Act is rolled out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: His question on ECT and expeditious settlement, I agree with him.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But I still do want to ask one more point around retrenchment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While I understand the need to balance, both the cost as well as the impact on employees, but because of the disruption we are seeing in the workplace and the restructuring of businesses, inevitably, there will be impact on employees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, have the tripartite partners come to some way of balancing both the cost and the protection for employees?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a very important area and the tripartite partners have had extensive deliberations on this issue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member, Mr Arasu 	Duraisamy, I think, articulated the thinking very well and, in fact, in a recent blog post, Mr Patrick Tay did likewise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I think it is useful for me to state it for the record.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From the employee's standpoint, any mandated minimum may become a norm even when employers are in a position to pay more and this would not benefit the workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From the employer's perspective, if the mandated minimum is too high, then the companies may not be able to afford and they may end up becoming over-burdened at the point in time when that sum of money could affect the remaining workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, since 1 January 2017, employers have been required to notify MOM of retrenchments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This enables Workforce Singapore, the unions and other relevant agencies to help the affected workers find alternative employment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I think that is a situation that is not too bad.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together?
